title: How he compiled
hookLine: a weaver, a leatherworker and a Sufi, side by side with the Gurus: how Guru Arjan chose what went into the book
last: ONE MASTER, CALLED GOSAIN AND ALLAH.

lines: A STACK OF PAGES, MANY HANDS.
WHAT GOES IN, WHAT STAYS OUT?
cards: A stack of handwritten pages, gathered from many hands. Some hold the Gurus' hymns, copied and recopied in different towns, a word drifting here and there.

Some hold songs by saints who were never Gurus: a weaver, a man who worked with hides, a Sufi from the Punjab. And tradition says some pages going around carried the Guru's name without the Guru's voice.
Somebody has to sit with all of it and decide what goes into one book, and what stays out. Today, Guru Arjan is the editor.

teach.h: THE GURU DICTATES, BHAI GURDAS WRITES.
teach.b: You've met the scribe, Bhai Gurdas, and the Gurus answering Farid; today, the editor's test.

Tradition says Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus before him, added his own, and dictated the volume to Bhai Gurdas, who wrote it out. The book became the Adi Granth, which later became the Guru Granth Sahib.
So what was his test? Not where a singer was born, which faith he grew up in, or whether his trade was respected.
The test was whether the hymn agreed with the Guru's teaching: the One, the Name, the turning away from ego. Look who passed.

teach.h: A WEAVER, A LEATHERWORKER, A SUFI.
teach.b: Kabir calls himself a weaver in his own verses. Ravidas names his people's work with hides and dead cattle, work his society looked down on, and sings that the learned now bow to him because of the Name.
Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, has his saloks near the end of the Granth. These aren't footnotes; they're sung in the gurdwara, in the same ragas as the Gurus' hymns.
And among Farid's saloks, a few verses are marked Mahala three and Mahala five: Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, answering.
Where one of Farid's lines could be heard too harshly, a Guru's line sits beside it, turning it a little.
So choosing carefully meant a wide welcome and a real conversation. The Guru didn't flatten the voices into one. He let them sing, and he answered.
His question wasn't, is this person like me? It was, does this agree with the truth?

how: In the gurdwara, the hymns of the Gurus and of the bhagats, such as Kabir, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid, are read and sung from the same Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bow to the whole as the Guru.

o: how the Guru kept only hymns by Sikhs born in Punjab
how Guru Arjan chose hymns by whether they fit the teaching
how the Granth was first printed for every gurdwara

games.q: who's in the book, and how: tap the pairs.
p: calls himself a weaver in his verses
names his people's work with hides
a Sufi whose saloks sit near the end
wrote the volume out, tradition says

s: the Granth holds only hymns by the Sikh Gurus
it also holds the bhagats: Kabir, Ravidas, Sheikh Farid and others, sung alongside the Gurus.
among Farid's saloks, some verses are marked as the Gurus answering
lines marked Mahala three and Mahala five sit beside his, turning them a little.
the test for a hymn was the singer's birth or faith
the test was whether it agreed with the Guru's teaching.

games.q: you're compiling a holy book. a song by a weaver from another tradition agrees with everything your Guru taught. what do you do?
o: leave it out: he isn't one of the Gurus.
put it in, and sing it with the Gurus' hymns.
keep it in a separate book of extras.
games.why: Guru Arjan put the bhagats' hymns in the same book, sung in the same ragas. what counted was whether a hymn agreed with the teaching.

practice: Let the voices of your week pass by, a podcast, a parent, a teacher, a song, a friend's text, without judging them yet. Then ask the editor's question of each: does this agree with the person I'm trying to become?
Keep the one that stands out, maybe from somewhere you didn't expect, and hold one thing it said.

wordCard.voice: How he compiled. Guru Arjan gathered many voices, Gurus and saints, and kept the ones that agreed with the Guru's teaching, whoever sang them. Today's word.

orig.note: the Word, the hymns; Sikhs speak of gurbani, the Guru's word, and of bhagat bani, the saints' hymns in the Granth.

carryVoice: Your line: he chose carefully. A wide welcome, and one test. I'll be here tomorrow.
